turns.reply: Welcome! You've seen gas pressure when pumping a bike tyre or squeezing a balloon, and it all comes down to tiny gas molecules moving randomly and constantly. Each time one strikes the wall of its container, it pushes on that wall with a tiny force. What do you think gas pressure is caused by?

Yes — molecules hitting the walls is exactly what causes gas pressure. Each single collision pushes on the wall with only a tiny force, but huge numbers of molecules collide every second, so the total effect is a steady pressure. If each collision is that tiny, why can we still measure a steady pressure?

turns.student: cos theres like millions of them hitting at once?
turns.reply: Yes — huge numbers of molecules hitting the walls is why the pressure is steady. If you heat a gas in a sealed rigid container, what happens to the speed of its molecules?
recap: Gas molecules move randomly and constantly, bumping into the container walls.
Each collision gives the wall a tiny push, a very small force.
So many molecules collide every second that the pushes add up.
That total effect is a steady pressure we can measure.

turns.reply: Yes — heating a gas makes its molecules move faster on average. Now, in a sealed rigid container the gas stays in the same space, which is what "constant volume" means. If the molecules in that sealed container are moving faster, what happens to the pressure?

turns.student: um does the pressure go down cos theres less space?
turns.reply: Not quite — the space doesn't shrink here. In a sealed rigid container the gas stays in the same space, so the molecules have the same room as before, but they are moving faster. How does that change how hard and how often they hit the walls?

turns.student: oh they hit harder and more often so pressure goes up?
turns.reply: Yes — faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure goes up. Now keep the temperature constant and squash a fixed mass of gas into half its volume. The same molecules now have less space, so they hit the walls twice as often. What happens to the pressure?
recap: Heating a gas makes its molecules move faster on average.
In a sealed rigid container, the volume stays the same.
Faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often.
So at constant volume, higher temperature means higher pressure.

turns.reply:
Fair, let me keep it short. Squash the gas into half the space and the molecules hit the walls twice as often, so the pressure doubles. That's because pressure × volume stays the same.

If the pressure starts at 100 kPa and the volume is halved, what is the new pressure?

No worries — the new pressure is 200 kPa, because halving the volume doubles it. That's called inversely proportional: when one quantity doubles, the other halves. If the volume of a gas is doubled at constant temperature, what happens to the pressure?

Yes — halving is right: doubling the volume halves the pressure. Next up: work is the transfer of energy by a force, and pushing a piston into a gas applies a force to it. So when you push that piston in, what is being transferred to the gas?
recap: Squash a gas into less space and the molecules hit the walls more often.
More frequent hits means higher pressure, as long as the temperature stays the same.
Pressure times volume stays constant, so halving the volume doubles the pressure.
That's inversely proportional: when one doubles, the other halves, just as you said.

turns.reply: That's okay. Think of it this way: when you push the piston in, your push passes energy into the gas, and we call that transfer "work". So the gas gains energy from your push. What is it that the gas gains when you do work on it?

Yes — energy is right: the gas gains energy from your push. That energy increases the gas's internal energy, which is the total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles. When the internal energy of the gas goes up, what can happen to its temperature?

No worries. Think of internal energy as the total energy of all the gas molecules added up, including the energy they have from moving. When your push gives the gas more energy, its molecules end up moving faster on average. So when the molecules move faster, what happens to the temperature of the gas?

The temperature goes up: faster molecules means a hotter gas. That brings us to the end of this lesson. You answered questions on "What causes gas pressure" and "Temperature and pressure at constant volume", answered some on "Pressure and volume at constant temperature" and "Doing work on a gas", and I told you the rest. Thanks for sticking with it.
recap: Work is energy transferred by a force, like pushing a piston.
Pushing the piston in transfers energy to the gas.
That extra energy raises the gas's internal energy.
More energy means the molecules move faster, so the gas heats up.

turns.reply: You're welcome. Remember the big idea: gas pressure is just countless tiny molecules crashing into the container walls. Bye for now, and come back any time!
